newsitem.title: UK: Oil markets can absorb Iraqi oil exports - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Oil markets can absorb Iraqi oil exports - analysts.

text.p: Iraq's possible return to the oil market will not lead to a sharp fall in prices and extra barrels from Iraq are likely to be absorbed by a hungry winter oil market, analysts said on Monday.

Both the United Nations and Iraq said on Monday that the way was clear for implementation of the oil-for-food deal under which Baghdad would be allowed to sell $2.0 billion worth of oil to buy food and medicines within weeks.

But oil analysts doubted whether the groundwork needed to bring Iraqi crude out of the ground and into export pipelines would be ready in time to meet Iraq's optimistic predictions of first oil in December.

"The thing is that if oil starts flowing, and it's a big if, prices will not remain at $23 a barrel if Iraq adds 700,000 bpd to global supplies," said Peter Bogin of Cambridge Energy Research Associates in Paris.
He expected prices to weaken though neither Bogin nor other analysts expected a big sell-off, given the market's immediate reaction to the news.
U.N. Secretary General Boutros Boutros-Ghali said on Monday he expected some movement on the Iraqi deal in the next few weeks but said there was still work to be done.

The agreement would allow partial exports of an estimated 600,000 to 700,000 barrels per day (bpd) of Iraqi crude oil at current prices, with U.N. monitors overseeing the exports and food distribution.

But Bogin and others did not expect the market to react too dramatically to the news, until at least the first Iraqi oil is on the water -- the first such exports since the U.N. imposed an embargo against Iraq after its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
World benchmark Brent crude from the North Sea fell an initial 40 cents on news of a deal but later scrambled back to trade only 18 cents down at $22.85 a barrel for January delivery.

"The market is hungry for barrels right now. I think for the time being we are in a world of status quo and I don't think prices are going to react sharply one way or another," said Peter Gignoux, head of the energy desk for Smith Barney in London.

The Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), of which Iraq is a member, is meeting in Vienna this week to agree production quotas for the next six months amid expectations it will freeze its ceiling.

OPEC raised its ceiling to 25.03 million bpd last June to make way for the return of partial Iraqi oil exports last September. OPEC admits that it is producing as much as one million bpd above its ceiling.

Bogin said if Iraqi exports reappeared in the first quarter of 1997 and OPEC over-producers continued to bleed oil onto the market, that would give an extra 1.7 million bpd in additional supplies, not to mention incremental oil from non-OPEC producers.
He said traders had already been burned when the deal was shelved in September after Iraqi President Saddam Hussein sent troops into northern Iraq to intervene in factional Kurdish fighting.
"Traders are saying that when the oil starts flowing or is on a ship, then they will believe it," Bogin said.

Oil refineries deliberately kept their stocks low, expecting prices to fall in September when Iraqi crude returned to the market. The delay meant some traders were caught short and had to buy at higher prices, pushing oil to a five-year high of $25.06 a barrel in October.
The average price for the year for front-month Brent has been $20 a barrel.

Bogin said that given low inventory levels in consuming countries, 26 million bpd from OPEC "would have been a comfortable number for OPEC to produce. If you raise it to 26.7 million bpd then obviously you are going to take a lot of steam out of the price."

He said non-OPEC supply was also expected to rise by 700,000 bpd above fourth quarter 1996 estimates. The market is also not expecting a huge stock draw in first quarter 1997 although its size would have an impact on prices.
"We are not expecting a huge stock draw in 1997 because of a fair amount of North Sea oil coming on," Bogin said.
But Bob Finch, head trader at Vitol SA, the world's biggest independent trading and refining company, said he believed the market could easily absorb the extra oil.
"The market is strong irrespective of Iraq. Spot market demand for winter fuels in the West is strong and stocks at refineries are low," he said.
Gignoux added: "I think for the time being we are in a world of status quo and I don't think prices are going to react sharply one way or another."
